title: Experience and Change
overview: Talk about what you have done and what is still changing. Work out which of the three jobs the present perfect is doing, and choose between it and the past simple by asking whether the time has finished. Describe a situation in movement rather than a fixed one, and compare how two people do something without calling either of them bad at it.
learningPath: The lesson: listen first, then read it back.
Words: five groups, 29 words. Listen and say each one.
Patterns: 5 cards. Read the one done for you before you try.
Reading: a worker's account, a language guide and a training record.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, listen back.
Writing: four tasks, each with a model.
Practice and the check: 7 exercises, then 12 questions.
functions: Say what you have done, without saying when
Say whether you are still somewhere, or have left
Describe a situation that is changing rather than fixed
Say whether something is temporary or permanent
Say something is difficult to do, or worth doing
Compare how two people work, without calling either one slow
Follow an account of how a job has changed over years
lectureScript:
This unit is about time, and about one choice in English that almost nobody gets right at first.

You have met the present perfect five times already.
Level 1 gave you have you ever. Level 2 gave you the finished action with no date, then yet and already, then how long, then since and for, then just.
So you can build the form. That is not the problem.
The problem is knowing when to choose it, and that is what this unit is for.

Start with what the form actually does. It does three separate jobs.
The first is recent. It happened a moment ago and it still matters now. I have just finished.
The second is indefinite. It happened, and when is not the point. I have worked in three countries.
The third is unfinished. It started in the past and it is still going. I have lived here for ten years.
That third job is the one to slow down for, because a great many languages have nothing like it.
I have lived here for ten years means I still live here.
I lived here for ten years means I do not.
Same ten years. Completely different claim about today.

Each job has words that give it away.
Just, recently and lately point at the recent job.
Ever, never and before point at the indefinite one.
For, since, so far and up to now point at the unfinished one.
Find that word first, and the form usually follows.

Now the choice itself, which is the second pattern.
The rule people are given is that the perfect is for recent things. That rule is wrong, and it is why the mistake survives.
The real question is whether the stretch of TIME is finished.
Have you seen her this week is correct, because this week is not over.
Did you see her last week is correct, because last week has closed.
Nothing there is about how recent the action was.
And that is why a date forces the past simple, always.
I have started this job in March is wrong. March has ended, so the sentence has to be I started this job in March.
If you want the perfect, drop the date: I have started a new job.

The third pattern moves the present continuous somewhere new.
You use it for now, and for an arrangement. Here it does a third job.
It describes a situation that is changing, over months or years.
Prices are rising. The work is getting harder. Fewer people are applying.
Compare those with prices rise, which would state it as a permanent fact about the world.
The continuous says it is in movement, and that is often exactly what you mean.
It also carries temporary against permanent.
I live in the north is where I am from. I am living with my sister at the moment is an arrangement that will end.
The usual warning applies. State verbs stay simple. I know him better now, never I am knowing him.

The fourth pattern fills a real gap.
You already know what follows a verb: hope to go, enjoy going.
Nothing below this unit told you what follows an ADJECTIVE, and the rules are different.
Most adjectives take to. Difficult to do. Ready to start. Likely to rain.
Two of them never do, and they are the ones everybody gets wrong.
Worth takes -ing. It is worth reading, never worth to read.
Busy takes -ing. She is busy working, never busy to work.
And any preposition after an adjective forces -ing. Capable of running. Tired of waiting. Keen on starting.
That last one is worth hearing twice, because keen appears in both shapes.
I am keen to start. I am keen on starting. Both correct, and the preposition is what decides.

The fifth pattern finishes something Level 2 and Unit 2 each did half of.
Level 2 gave you more slowly and harder. Unit 2 of this level gave you not as good as, for adjectives.
Here it is adverbs, and the negative frame.
He does not work as quickly as she does.
That says he is slower, and it says it without the word slow appearing anywhere.
There is also less, which is blunter: he works less carefully than she does.
And the same warning as before. Never very in front of a comparative. Much, far, a lot, slightly.

The reading is an account by somebody who has stood at the same bench for twenty years and watched everything else move.
Watch the verbs in it. Almost every choice in that text is deliberate.
Start with the words. Say each one aloud before you move on.

words.meaning: To grow or change into something more complete.
words.example: The town developed slowly after the railway came.
practice: She has developed a real feel for the work.
The situation is developing faster than anybody expected.
Develop takes into for what a thing becomes.
Its noun is development, with no extra e.
words.tutor: Say one skill you have developed. Ask the tutor to check the perfect form.

words.meaning: To become larger, or to make something larger.
words.example: The company has expanded twice since I joined.
practice: They are expanding into two more towns.
Expand takes into for a new area.
Metal expands when it is heated.
Its noun is expansion, not expandment.
words.tutor: Say what has expanded where you work or live. Ask the tutor about the noun form.

words.meaning: To become smaller, weaker or less; or to refuse politely.
words.example: The number of applicants has declined every year.
practice: Sales have been declining since the spring.
She declined the offer, politely but firmly.
Decline is the formal opposite of grow and of accept.
As a noun: a steady decline in numbers.
words.tutor: Say what has declined. Ask the tutor which of the two meanings you used.

words.meaning: To change something completely, so it is hard to recognise.
words.example: The new roof transformed the building.
practice: The area has been transformed in ten years.
Transform is much stronger than change.
It takes into: transformed into workshops.
Its noun is transformation.
words.tutor: Say what transformed something. Ask the tutor whether transform was too strong.

words.meaning: To change yourself or a thing to fit new conditions.
words.example: It took me a year to adapt to the shifts.
practice: They adapted the machine for a different job.
Adapt takes to for the new conditions.
Adapting is not the same as accepting.
Its noun is adaptation.
words.tutor: Say what you had to adapt to. Ask the tutor to check you said adapt TO.

words.meaning: To make a small change so a thing fits or works better.
words.example: I adjusted the strap and it was fine.
practice: It takes a few weeks to adjust to a new routine.
Adjust is a small change; adapt is a bigger one.
Adjust also takes to for conditions.
Its noun is adjustment.
words.tutor: Say what you adjusted. Ask the tutor whether adjust or adapt was the right size of change.

words.meaning: The length of time something lasts.
words.example: The duration of the course is eighteen months.
practice: For the duration of the works, the road is closed.
Duration is formal: in speech you would say how long.
It answers how long, not when.
The duration of, not the duration for.
words.tutor: Say the duration of something. Ask the tutor whether duration suited the register.

words.meaning: A length of time with a beginning and an end.
words.example: There was a long period when nothing happened.
practice: Over a period of six months, the numbers halved.
A period is defined by what happened in it.
Period is far commoner than duration in speech.
A trial period is a set time for testing something.
words.tutor: Describe a period in your life. Ask the tutor to check the tense.

words.meaning: Ten years.
words.example: The mill stood empty for a decade.
practice: Over the last decade, the town has changed completely.
A decade is ten years; a century is a hundred.
The stress is on the first part: DEC-ade.
It often goes with the present perfect: for a decade.
words.tutor: Say what has changed over a decade. Ask the tutor to check the perfect form.

words.meaning: A long period of history with its own character.
words.example: That was the end of an era for the industry.
practice: We are living through a difficult era.
An era is defined by its character, a decade only by its length.
The end of an era is a fixed phrase.
It is pronounced EAR-a.
words.starter: It was the end of an era for …
words.tutor: Use era about a period with its own character. Ask the tutor whether era or period fitted.

words.meaning: Lasting for a limited time only.
words.example: I took a temporary job for the summer.
practice: The arrangement is temporary and everybody knows it.
Temporary work often becomes permanent.
The present continuous suits temporary situations.
Its adverb is temporarily.
words.tutor: Describe a temporary arrangement. Ask the tutor which tense you used.

words.meaning: Lasting for all the time you can see ahead.
words.example: After two years they made the post permanent.
practice: Nothing here is permanent, whatever they tell you.
Permanent is the opposite of temporary.
The present simple suits permanent situations.
Its adverb is permanently.
words.tutor: Say when something became permanent. Ask the tutor to check the tense against the meaning.

words.meaning: To reach the standard that lets you do something officially.
words.example: She qualified as an electrician last year.
practice: I have qualified, but I have not started yet.
Qualify takes as before the job.
You can also qualify FOR something: for a grant.
Its noun is qualification.
words.tutor: Say what you qualified as, or would like to. Ask the tutor to check as or for.

words.meaning: To succeed in doing something that took effort.
words.example: We accomplished more in a week than I expected.
practice: She has accomplished a great deal since then.
Accomplish is more formal than manage or do.
Its noun is accomplishment, close to achievement.
It suits a report better than a conversation.
words.tutor: Say what you accomplished. Ask the tutor whether accomplish suited the register.

words.meaning: To learn something so well that you do it without effort.
words.example: It takes years to master a trade.
practice: I have never quite mastered the spelling.
Master is stronger than learn: it means completely.
It is also a noun: a master of the trade.
Mastering something is the end of a long process.
words.tutor: Say something you have never mastered. Ask the tutor to check the perfect form.

words.meaning: To get something useful, usually over time.
words.example: I gained a lot of experience that year.
practice: She has gained confidence since she started.
Gain suits things that build up: experience, weight, speed.
It is the opposite of lose.
As a noun: a gain in speed.
words.tutor: Say what you gained from something. Ask the tutor whether gain or get was better.

words.meaning: To come to have something, often slowly or by effort.
words.example: He acquired the skill by watching.
practice: I have acquired a taste for it.
Acquire is the formal word for get.
Acquired takes no preposition: acquire a skill.
Its noun is acquisition.
words.tutor: Say what you acquired and how. Ask the tutor whether acquire sounded too formal.

words.meaning: To keep following something you want, over a long time.
words.example: She pursued a career in engineering.
practice: I have pursued it for years without much luck.
Pursue suits a career, a claim, a qualification.
It is pronounced per-SUE.
Its noun is pursuit.
words.tutor: Say what you decided to pursue. Ask the tutor to check the form after decided.

words.meaning: Happening a short time ago.
words.example: There has been a recent change to the rules.
practice: In recent years the work has got harder.
Recent goes with the present perfect very often.
Its adverb is recently: I have recently moved.
Recent is about the past; current is about now.
words.tutor: Say what has changed recently. Ask the tutor to check the perfect form.

words.meaning: Still happening, and not finished.
words.example: The investigation is ongoing.
practice: There is an ongoing problem with the heating.
Ongoing suits the present continuous.
It is written as one word.
An ongoing issue has no end date yet.
words.tutor: Describe an ongoing situation. Ask the tutor which tense fitted.

words.meaning: Existing now, at this moment.
words.example: The current rate is lower than last year's.
practice: My current job is temporary.
Current is now; recent is just past.
Its adverb is currently: I am currently studying.
Current is also a noun: the current in a river.
words.tutor: Describe your current situation. Ask the tutor whether current or recent was right.

words.meaning: Belonging to an earlier time; the one before this.
words.example: My former employer still owes me a reference.
practice: The former manager left in March.
Former is the opposite of current.
It goes straight before the noun: a former colleague.
Formerly is the adverb: formerly a school.
words.tutor: Describe something former. Ask the tutor to check the word order.

words.meaning: The most recent so far, with more expected.
words.example: The latest figures came out on Monday.
practice: Have you seen the latest version?
Latest means most recent; last means final.
The latest news is not the last news.
It often goes with the present perfect.
words.tutor: Describe the latest version of something. Ask the tutor about latest and last.

words.meaning: Happening all the time, without stopping.
words.example: There was a constant noise from the yard.
practice: The constant changes made it hard to plan.
Constant suits things that do not let up.
Its adverb is constantly.
Constantly + -ing often shows irritation.
words.tutor: Describe something constant. Ask the tutor whether it sounded like a complaint.

groups.title: The words that go with the perfect

words.meaning: Up to this point, with more still to come.
words.example: So far the work has gone well.
practice: We have had three replies so far.
So far signals that the story is not finished.
It goes at the start or the end, rarely the middle.
So far, so good is a fixed phrase.
words.tutor: Say what you have done so far. Ask the tutor to check the perfect form.

words.meaning: Continuously, from that moment until now.
words.example: I have worked here ever since.
practice: Ever since the closure, the town has been quieter.
Ever since is stronger than since: it stresses the whole stretch.
It can stand alone at the end of a sentence.
It always reaches up to now, so it takes the perfect.
words.tutor: Use ever since about your own life. Ask the tutor to check both halves.

words.meaning: Until this moment, with the situation still open.
words.example: Up to now nobody has complained.
practice: Up to now the plan has worked.
It means the same as so far and is slightly more formal.
It usually starts the sentence.
It takes the present perfect.
words.tutor: Say what has been true up to now. Ask the tutor to check the tense.

words.meaning: In the recent past, up to now.
words.example: I have not seen much of her lately.
practice: Lately the trains have been worse.
Lately means the same as recently but is commoner in the negative.
It goes at the start or the end.
It takes the present perfect, not the past simple.
words.tutor: Say what has been happening lately. Ask the tutor to check you used the perfect.

words.meaning: Before now, and sooner than expected.
words.example: I have already sent it.
practice: Have you finished already?
Already sits between have and the past form.
In a question it shows surprise.
Already is for what HAS happened; yet is for what has not.
words.tutor: Say what you have already done. Ask the tutor where you put already.

grammar.title: One form, three jobs: what the present perfect is actually saying
grammar.explanation:
You already build this form and you have met it five times.
What no unit has done is say WHY you would choose it.
have or has plus the past form does three separate jobs, and knowing which
one you are in is what stops the mistakes further down.
grammar.rule:
JOB 1 — recent. It happened a moment ago and still matters.
I have just finished. She has only recently qualified.

JOB 2 — indefinite. It happened, and WHEN is not the point.
I have worked in three countries. Have you ever driven a van?

JOB 3 — unfinished. It started in the past and is still true.
I have lived here for ten years. She has worked here since March.

The words that give the job away:
recent      just, recently, lately
indefinite  ever, never, before, three times
unfinished  for, since, so far, up to now, ever since

Job 3 is the one that has no equivalent in many languages.
I have lived here for ten years means I still live here.
I lived here for ten years means I do not any more.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Which job is this, and is it right? I have worked here since 2019.
1. Look for the giveaway word. since.
2. since belongs to job 3, unfinished.
3. So the sentence claims I still work here.
4. That is what the speaker means, so the form is right.
Answer: job 3, and correct.
If they had left in 2022 they would need the past simple: I worked there from 2019 to 2022.
grammar.mistake:
Using job 3 for a finished stretch tells the listener you are still there.
No: I have worked there for two years. (said about an old job)
Yes: I worked there for two years.
The perfect reaches up to now. If you have left, it cannot.
grammar.tip: Find the giveaway word first. It tells you which of the three jobs you are in.
grammar.practice:
Name the job — recent, indefinite or unfinished — for each sentence.
1. I have just finished the report.
2. I have lived here for ten years.
3. Have you ever worked nights?
4. She has worked here since March.
5. We have had three replies so far.
6. He has recently qualified.
Now decide whether each of these means the person is still there.
7. I have worked at the depot for six years.
8. I worked at the depot for six years.
grammar.answers:
1. recent  2. unfinished  3. indefinite  4. unfinished
5. unfinished  6. recent
7. Still there. The perfect reaches up to now.
8. Not there any more. The past simple closes it off.
Numbers 7 and 8 are the whole point of the card.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: I have worked there, or I worked there: choosing between the two
grammar.explanation:
This is the choice the last card was building towards.
Both forms are correct English. They are not interchangeable.
The question is never which is more polite. It is whether the time is finished.
grammar.rule:
PRESENT PERFECT when the time is still open:
I have worked here for six years.   (I am still here)
I have been to three meetings today. (today is not over)
Have you seen her this week?         (the week is not over)

PAST SIMPLE when the time is closed:
I worked there for six years.       (I left)
I went to three meetings yesterday. (yesterday is over)
Did you see her last week?          (last week is over)

A definite past time FORCES the past simple:
yesterday, last year, in 2019, when I was twenty, ago
NOT: I have finished it yesterday.
YES: I finished it yesterday.

The commonest real conversation uses both, in this order:
Have you ever worked nights?  (indefinite, opens it)
Yes, I worked nights for two years in my twenties. (definite, fills it in)
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Choose the form: I ___ (finish) it yesterday.
1. Look for a time expression. yesterday.
2. Is that time finished? Yes, completely.
3. A finished time forces the past simple.
Answer: I finished it yesterday.
I have finished it yesterday is wrong, however recent it feels.
grammar.mistake:
A definite past time and the present perfect cannot share a sentence.
No: I have started this job in March.
Yes: I started this job in March.
Or, without the date: I have started a new job.
grammar.tip: Ask whether the TIME is finished, not whether the action is.
grammar.practice:
Choose the present perfect or the past simple.
1. I ___ (finish) it yesterday.
2. I ___ (work) here for six years, and I am still here.
3. She ___ (leave) in 2019.
4. ___ you ___ (see) her this week?
5. We ___ (have) three replies so far.
6. He ___ (qualify) when he was twenty-two.
7. The town ___ (change) completely over the last decade.
8. I ___ (not speak) to him since the meeting.
grammar.answers:
1. finished  2. have worked  3. left  4. Have you seen
5. have had  6. qualified  7. has changed  8. have not spoken
Numbers 1, 3 and 6 all carry a finished time, which forces the past simple.
Numbers 2, 5, 7 and 8 all reach up to now.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Prices are rising: the present continuous for a situation that is changing
grammar.explanation:
You use this form for now (I am eating) and for an arrangement (I am meeting her on Tuesday).
It has a third job that Levels 1 and 2 did not cover.
It describes a situation that is CHANGING, over weeks or years rather than minutes.
grammar.rule:
A situation changing over a long stretch:
Prices are rising.
The work is getting harder every year.
Fewer people are applying than they used to.
The town is changing faster than anybody expected.

The verbs that go with it: rise, fall, grow, improve, get, become, increase, decline.

TEMPORARY against PERMANENT:
I am living with my sister at the moment.  (temporary)
I live in the north.                       (permanent)
She is working in the warehouse this month. (temporary)
She works in the warehouse.                 (her job)

And a use that carries feeling, with always or constantly:
He is always losing his keys. (this is a complaint, not a fact)
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Choose the form: The work ___ (get) harder every year.
1. Is this one moment, a permanent fact, or a change over time?
2. Every year means it is moving, so it is a change.
3. A changing situation takes the present continuous.
Answer: The work is getting harder every year.
The work gets harder every year would state it as a permanent fact, which is a different claim.
grammar.mistake:
A state verb does not take this form, however temporary the state.
No: I am knowing him better now.
Yes: I know him better now.
know, own, believe, understand and prefer all stay simple.
grammar.tip: Is it moving? Continuous. Is it just true? Simple.
grammar.practice:
Choose the present simple or the present continuous.
1. Prices ___ (rise) faster than wages.
2. I ___ (live) in the north. (it is permanent)
3. I ___ (live) with my sister at the moment.
4. The work ___ (get) harder every year.
5. She ___ (work) in the warehouse. (it is her job)
6. I ___ (know) him better now.
7. Fewer people ___ (apply) than they used to.
8. The investigation ___ (be) ongoing.
grammar.answers:
1. are rising  2. live  3. am living  4. is getting
5. works  6. know  7. are applying  8. is
Wrong on 6 or 8? know and be are state verbs and stay simple.
Numbers 2, 3 and 5 turn on temporary against permanent, not on time.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: Difficult to do, worth doing: what follows an adjective
grammar.explanation:
Levels 1 and 2 taught what follows a VERB: hope to go, enjoy going.
Adjectives have the same choice and a different set of rules, and nothing
below this unit covers them. Most adjectives take to. A few take -ing,
and a preposition after an adjective always takes -ing.
grammar.rule:
Most adjectives take TO:
difficult to do, easy to say, ready to start, willing to help
likely to rain, keen to begin, glad to hear it

worth and busy take -ING, with no to at all:
It is worth doing.   NOT worth to do.
She is busy working. NOT busy to work.

A PREPOSITION after the adjective always takes -ing:
keen ON starting, capable OF running, tired OF waiting
interested IN learning, afraid OF asking

Watch the pair that looks the same and is not:
I am keen to start.       (adjective + to)
I am keen on starting.    (adjective + preposition + -ing)
Both are correct. The preposition is what decides the form.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Fill the gap: The report is worth ___ (read).
1. Which adjective is it? worth.
2. worth is one of the two that never take to.
3. So the verb takes -ing.
Answer: The report is worth reading.
worth to read is the error, and it is common because every neighbouring adjective takes to.
grammar.mistake:
worth is the one everybody gets wrong, because difficult, easy and ready all take to.
No: It is worth to read.
Yes: It is worth reading.
Same for busy: she is busy working, never busy to work.
grammar.tip: Is there a preposition? Then -ing. No preposition? Almost always to, except worth and busy.
grammar.practice:
Write the right form of the verb in brackets.
1. The report is worth ___ (read).
2. It is difficult ___ (explain).
3. I am keen ___ (start) next month.
4. I am keen on ___ (start) next month.
5. She is busy ___ (write) the report.
6. He is capable of ___ (run) the whole shift.
7. Are you ready ___ (go)?
8. I am tired of ___ (wait).
grammar.answers:
1. reading  2. to explain  3. to start  4. starting
5. writing  6. running  7. to go  8. waiting
Numbers 3 and 4 are the pair: the same adjective, and the preposition in 4 forces -ing.
Numbers 1 and 5 are worth and busy, the two that never take to.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: He does not work as quickly: comparing HOW somebody does it
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 gave you more slowly and the most carefully, and harder and sooner.
Unit 2 of this level did the same job for adjectives.
This card does the half neither of them reached: the NEGATIVE comparison,
and less, on adverbs.
grammar.rule:
The comparison you already have:
She works more carefully than I do.
He finished sooner than expected.

The NEGATIVE frame, which says the same thing more gently:
He does not work as quickly as she does.
It did not go as smoothly as we hoped.
not nearly as quickly = a much bigger gap

LESS, the direct opposite of more:
He works less carefully than she does.
far less carefully, much less often, considerably less clearly

The degree words are the same as for adjectives:
much, far, a lot, slightly, considerably
NOT very: never very more quickly.

Irregular adverbs keep their own forms:
well -> better -> best      badly -> worse -> worst
She did it better than I did. He took it worse than expected.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Say this more gently: He works more slowly than she does.
1. The negative frame needs the SLOWER person first, and slowly becomes quickly.
2. The frame is not as ... as.
3. He does not work as quickly as she does.
Answer: He does not work as quickly as she does.
Same fact, and nobody has been called slow.
grammar.mistake:
very cannot sit in front of a comparative adverb, exactly as with adjectives.
No: She works very more carefully.
Yes: She works much more carefully.
And it is less carefully, never more less carefully.
grammar.tip: not as ... as is the polite comparison. less is the blunt one. Neither takes very.
grammar.practice:
Rewrite each one using not as ... as. The order will flip.
1. He works more slowly than she does.
2. The second route is worse than the first.
3. She explained it more clearly than he did.
Now use less.
4. He checks his work ___ carefully than she does.
5. It happens ___ often than it used to.
Now correct these.
6. She works very more carefully.
7. He did it more better than expected.
grammar.answers:
1. He does not work as quickly as she does.
2. The second route is not as good as the first.
3. He did not explain it as clearly as she did.
4. less  5. less
6. She works much more carefully.  7. He did it better than expected.
Numbers 1, 2 and 3 all swap which person or thing comes first, and 1 and 3 swap the adverb too.
5 or more right: good.

readings.title: Twenty Years at the Same Bench
readings.setting: A workshop, told by somebody still working there
readings.passage:
I have worked at the same bench for twenty years, and almost nothing about the job is the same.
When I started, everything was measured by hand and written on a card.
Now the measurements come off a screen, and the cards went years ago.
I qualified in 1998, which felt like the end of the learning.
It was not. The work has changed three times since then, and I have had to adapt each time.
The first change was difficult to accept. The second was easier, because I had seen one already.
Younger people are arriving with skills I never had, and that is fine.
What they do not have is the twenty years, and there is no way to acquire that quickly.
Numbers in the trade have declined steadily. We were forty when I started and we are eleven now.
The work itself is not disappearing. It is changing, which is not the same thing.
Up to now I have always found something worth learning at the start of each year.
The day that stops is the day I will go.

readings.title: Have You Finished, or Did You Finish?
readings.setting: A page from a language guide
readings.passage:
Speakers of many languages find one English choice harder than any other.
I have finished and I finished are both correct, and they are not the same.
The rule is not about how recent the action is. It is about whether the TIME is finished.
If the stretch of time is still open, English uses the perfect.
I have seen her this week works, because the week is not over.
Did you see her last week uses the past, because last week has closed.
This is why a date forces the past simple.
I have started this job in March is wrong, however recently March was, because March has ended.
A useful test is to ask what the sentence claims about now.
I have lived here for ten years claims you still live here.
I lived here for ten years claims you do not.
Neither is more polite or more formal than the other. They say different things, and a listener hears the difference.

readings.title: Continuing Training Record: Annual Return
readings.passage:
CONTINUING TRAINING RECORD
Member: R. Okonjo        Membership number: 41-2288
Period covered: 1 April to 31 March

Hours completed so far this period: 24 of the required 30

Courses attended
  Safe isolation, refresher            6 hours   completed
  Updated wiring regulations          12 hours   completed
  Fault diagnosis, part one            6 hours   completed
  Fault diagnosis, part two            6 hours   booked for 14 March

Has your scope of work changed during this period?  Yes
If yes, describe: I have taken on commercial work, which I had not done previously.

Members who have not completed 30 hours by 31 March are moved to inactive status.
Inactive members may return at any time once the outstanding hours have been completed.
Hours completed above 30 do not carry over to the following period.

comprehension.q: How long has the writer worked at the same bench?
comprehension.why: The first line, and the perfect form tells you they are still there.

comprehension.q: How many people were in the trade when the writer started, and how many now?
Why was the second change easier than the first?
comprehension.a: Because the writer had already been through one.
comprehension.why: The text gives the reason in the same sentence.

comprehension.q: 'I have worked at the same bench for twenty years.' Does the writer still work there? How do you know?
comprehension.a: Yes. The present perfect with for reaches up to now.
comprehension.why: This is the unfinished use. The past simple would mean they had left.

comprehension.q: The writer says the work is changing rather than disappearing. Why does that distinction matter to them?
comprehension.a: Because a changing trade still has a future, and there is still something to learn.
comprehension.why: The next line says they have always found something worth learning.

comprehension.q: According to the article, what is the choice actually about?
comprehension.a: Whether the period of time is finished, not how recent the action is.
comprehension.why: Stated in the third and fourth lines.

comprehension.q: Why is 'I have started this job in March' wrong?
comprehension.a: Because March has ended, and a finished time forces the past simple.
comprehension.why: The article says a date forces the past simple, however recent it is.

comprehension.q: The article says neither form is 'more polite'. What does it say the difference is?
comprehension.a: They say different things, and a listener hears the difference.
comprehension.why: The last line. It is a difference of meaning, not of register.

comprehension.q: R. Okonjo has 24 hours. What happens if the March course is missed?
comprehension.a: They would have 24 of 30 and be moved to inactive status.
comprehension.why: The rule at the foot of the form, applied to the hours listed.

comprehension.q: Somebody completes 36 hours this period. How many carry over to next year?
comprehension.a: None. Hours above 30 do not carry over.
comprehension.why: The last line of the form says so directly.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Three things you have done, three you did
speaking.instructions:
Say six sentences about your own life, real or invented.
The first three use the present perfect, with no date.
The last three use the past simple, each with a definite time.
A model, so you can hear the pair:
I have worked in three different towns.
I have never driven a lorry.
I have just finished a course.
I moved here in 2019.
I qualified when I was twenty-four.
I finished the last module in March.
Tap the mic. Say your six sentences. Tap again and listen.
Check: do the first three have NO date in them?
Does every one of the last three have a definite time?
speaking.tutor: Say your six sentences and ask the tutor whether any date slipped into the first three.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — The weak have you cannot hear
speaking.instructions:
In the present perfect, have and has are almost never stressed.
They shrink, and they join on to the word in front.
Listen and repeat. The capital letters show where the stress goes.
I have finished     sounds like  I-ve FINished
She has gone        sounds like  She-z GONE
We have never been  sounds like  We-ve NEVer been
Have you seen it?   sounds like  v-you SEEN it?
The respelling is a hint for your ear. Always write I have or I've.
Now say these three lines.
I have worked here for six years.
She has just finished the course.
Have you ever worked nights?
Tap the mic. Say the three lines. Tap again and listen.
Check: is have quiet and joined to the word before it?
If you hear a strong HAVE, say the line again faster.
speaking.tutor: Say the three lines and ask the tutor whether have sounded weak or stressed.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — What is changing where you are
speaking.instructions:
Say five sentences about something that is changing: your town, your trade, your family.
Every sentence must use the present continuous for a change over time.
Useful verbs: rising, falling, getting, becoming, changing, improving.
A model, so you can hear the shape:
Rents are rising faster than wages here.
The high street is getting quieter every year.
Fewer young people are staying after school.
The work itself is changing rather than disappearing.
Things are improving slowly, but only slowly.
Tap the mic. Say your five sentences. Tap again and listen.
Check: is every verb in the continuous?
Does each sentence describe a MOVEMENT rather than a fixed fact?
speaking.tutor: Describe the change to the tutor and ask whether any sentence should have been simple instead.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Listen: how the job changed
speaking.instructions:
Tap Listen. Do not read along. Listen twice.
I have been at the depot since 2011, so that is thirteen years.
When I started, we sorted everything by hand and the shift finished at four.
The sorting is done by machine now, and the shifts are longer.
Numbers have fallen, but the volume has actually gone up.
I have had to learn the system twice, because they replaced it in 2019.
It is getting harder to find people who will stay more than a year.
Up to now I have not thought seriously about leaving.
Now answer. Tap the mic and say each answer.
1. How long has the speaker been at the depot?
2. What is done by machine now?
3. Why did the speaker have to learn the system twice?
4. What is getting harder?
Tap again and listen to your answers.
Check: 1 thirteen years, since 2011. 2 the sorting.
3 the system was replaced in 2019. 4 finding people who stay more than a year.
speaking.tutor: Retell what changed at the depot in four sentences, then ask the tutor what you left out.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Say it more gently
speaking.instructions:
Each line below is true and blunt. Say it again using not as ... as.
The two things will swap places, and often the adjective or adverb flips too.
1. He works more slowly than she does.
2. The second route is worse than the first.
3. She explained it more clearly than he did.
4. This year was harder than last year.
A model for the first one:
He does not work as quickly as she does.
Tap the mic. Say all four gently. Tap again and listen.
Check: in each one, did the two things change places?
Did you avoid saying anybody was slow, bad or unclear?
speaking.tutor: Say your four gentler versions and ask the tutor whether any still sounded blunt.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Two minutes: what you have gained
speaking.instructions:
Speak for two minutes about what you have gained from a job, a course or a place.
Cover these four, in this order:
what you have learned
what you have never mastered
what is changing now
what you would like to pursue next
Use the present perfect for the first two and the present continuous for the third.
Tap the mic. Speak for two minutes without stopping.
Tap again and listen to the whole thing.
Check: did you keep the perfect out of the third part?
Did any definite date slip into a perfect sentence?
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor your two minutes and ask where a tense went wrong.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Six sentences about what has changed
writing.prompt:
Write six sentences about how a place or a job has changed.
Three must use the present perfect for something that reaches up to now.
Three must use the past simple, each with a definite time.
Use at least three of: so far, ever since, up to now, lately, already.
writing.model:
The trade has changed thrice since I started.
Numbers have declined steadily, and they are still falling.
Up to now I have always found something new to learn each year.
I qualified in 1998, which felt like the end of the learning.
They replaced the whole system in 2019.
We were forty when I started, and last year we were eleven.
writing.criteria:
Three present perfect sentences, none carrying a definite date.
Three past simple sentences, each with a definite time.
Three or more of the perfect time phrases used.
No sentence longer than twenty words.
writing.support: Write the six times first — three open, three closed — then write a sentence for each.
writing.extension: Add a seventh sentence in the present continuous, about what is changing right now.

writing.title: Writing 2 — A paragraph about something that is changing
writing.prompt:
Write one paragraph about a situation that is changing.
Use the present continuous at least four times for the movement.
Use the present simple at least once for something that is simply true.
writing.model:
Rents here are rising faster than wages, and the gap is getting wider every year.
Fewer young people are staying after school, because the work is not here.
The high street is emptying slowly rather than suddenly.
The town is not dying. It is changing, which is a different thing.
What it needs is time, and nobody is offering that.
writing.length: One paragraph, five to seven sentences.
writing.criteria:
Present continuous used at least four times for a change over time.
Present simple used at least once for a plain fact.
No state verb put in the continuous.
It reads as a paragraph, not a list.
writing.support: List four things that are moving, then write one sentence for each and join them.
writing.extension: Add a sentence with a comparative adverb: faster than, less often than.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Five sentences that follow an adjective
writing.prompt:
Write five sentences about your learning, each built on one of these adjectives:
difficult, worth, keen, capable, tired.
Watch which of them takes to, which takes -ing, and which takes a preposition.
writing.model:
The spelling was difficult to learn and I still get it wrong.
The extra course was worth doing, even though it cost me a weekend.
I am keen to start the next part in the spring.
I am not yet capable of running a job on my own.
I am tired of explaining the same thing twice.
writing.criteria:
All five adjectives used.
worth followed by -ing, with no to.
capable and tired each followed by of and an -ing form.
difficult and keen each followed by to and a plain verb.
writing.support: Write the five adjectives down the page first and put the right little word beside each.
writing.extension: Add a sixth sentence using keen ON doing, and say how it differs from keen TO do.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Fill in the training record
writing.prompt:
You are completing the annual return in Reading 3. Invent the trade and the courses.
Fill in every field. List four courses and give the hours.
The scope-of-work field must use a present perfect sentence.
writing.model:
Member: A. Duarte        Membership number: 52-7741
Period covered: 1 April to 31 March
Hours completed so far this period: 26 of the required 30
Courses attended
  Manual handling, refresher        4 hours   completed
  New labelling standards          10 hours   completed
  Cold storage, part one            6 hours   completed
  Cold storage, part two            6 hours   booked for 20 March
Has your scope of work changed during this period? Yes
If yes, describe: I have moved onto night deliveries, which I had not done before.
writing.length: A completed form, about seven fields.
writing.criteria:
Every field on the form answered.
The hours in the list add up to the total given.
The scope-of-work answer uses the present perfect.
No definite date inside that perfect sentence.
writing.support: Copy the shape of Reading 3 line by line and change only the content.
writing.extension: Add two sentences saying what you will do if you do not reach thirty hours.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Which job is the perfect doing?
activities.instructions:
Write recent, indefinite or unfinished beside each one.
1. I have just finished the report.
2. I have lived here for ten years.
3. Have you ever worked nights?
4. She has worked here since March.
5. We have had three replies so far.
6. He has recently qualified.
7. I have never driven a van.
8. The town has changed a great deal lately.
activities.answers:
1. recent  2. unfinished  3. indefinite  4. unfinished
5. unfinished  6. recent  7. indefinite  8. recent
The giveaway word does the work every time: just, for, ever, since, so far, recently, never, lately.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Write the eight, then circle the giveaway word in each before you name the job.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Perfect or past?
activities.instructions:
Choose the present perfect or the past simple.
1. I ___ (finish) it yesterday.
2. I ___ (work) here for six years, and I am still here.
3. She ___ (leave) in 2019.
4. ___ you ___ (see) her this week?
5. We ___ (have) three replies so far.
6. He ___ (qualify) when he was twenty-two.
7. The town ___ (change) completely over the last decade.
8. I ___ (not speak) to him since the meeting.
9. They ___ (replace) the system in 2019.
10. I ___ (never drive) a lorry.
activities.answers:
1. finished  2. have worked  3. left  4. Have you seen  5. have had
6. qualified  7. has changed  8. have not spoken  9. replaced  10. have never driven
1, 3, 6 and 9 all carry a finished time, which forces the past simple.
The rest all reach up to now, or carry no time at all.
8 or more right: good.
activities.solo: For each one, underline the time expression first. If there is none, the perfect is usually right.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Simple or continuous?
activities.instructions:
Choose the present simple or the present continuous.
1. Prices ___ (rise) faster than wages.
2. I ___ (live) in the north. (permanent)
3. I ___ (live) with my sister at the moment.
4. The work ___ (get) harder every year.
5. She ___ (work) in the warehouse. (it is her job)
6. I ___ (know) him better now.
7. Fewer people ___ (apply) than they used to.
8. The investigation ___ (be) ongoing.
9. He ___ (always lose) his keys. (you are complaining)
10. Metal ___ (expand) when it is heated.
activities.answers:
1. are rising  2. live  3. am living  4. is getting  5. works
6. know  7. are applying  8. is  9. is always losing  10. expands
6 and 8 are state verbs and stay simple. 10 is a permanent fact, so simple.
9 is the continuous used to complain, which is why always is there.
8 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Ask of each: is this moving, is it temporary, or is it just true?

activities.title: Practice 4 — After the adjective
activities.instructions:
Write the right form of the verb in brackets.
1. The report is worth ___ (read).
2. It is difficult ___ (explain).
3. I am keen ___ (start) next month.
4. I am keen on ___ (start) next month.
5. She is busy ___ (write) the report.
6. He is capable of ___ (run) the whole shift.
7. Are you ready ___ (go)?
8. I am tired of ___ (wait).
9. It is likely ___ (rain).
10. I am interested in ___ (learn) more about it.
activities.answers:
1. reading  2. to explain  3. to start  4. starting  5. writing
6. running  7. to go  8. waiting  9. to rain  10. learning
Every -ing in this list follows either a preposition (4, 6, 8, 10) or worth and busy (1, 5).
Everything else takes to.
8 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Before writing, mark each line P if there is a preposition and W if the adjective is worth or busy.

activities.title: Practice 5 — The gentler comparison
activities.instructions:
Rewrite each one using not as ... as. The order will flip.
1. He works more slowly than she does.
2. The second route is worse than the first.
3. She explained it more clearly than he did.
4. This year was harder than last year.
Now use less.
5. He checks his work ___ carefully than she does.
6. It happens ___ often than it used to.
Now correct these.
7. She works very more carefully.
8. He did it more better than expected.
activities.answers:
1. He does not work as quickly as she does.
2. The second route is not as good as the first.
3. He did not explain it as clearly as she did.
4. Last year was not as hard as this year.
5. less  6. less
7. She works much more carefully.  8. He did it better than expected.
Numbers 1 and 3 flip the adverb as well as the order: slowly becomes quickly, and the person changes.
6 or more right: good.
activities.solo: Write both versions side by side and read each pair aloud. Decide which you would say to the person's face.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Correct the tense
activities.instructions:
Each sentence has one tense error. Write it correctly.
1. I have started this job in March.
2. I have worked there for two years, but I left in 2020.
3. Did you see her this week?
4. I am knowing him better now.
5. The work gets harder every year, and it is still moving.
6. It is worth to read.
activities.answers:
1. I started this job in March. (a date forces the past simple)
2. I worked there for two years. (you left, so the time is closed)
3. Have you seen her this week? (this week is not over)
4. I know him better now. (know is a state verb)
5. The work is getting harder every year. (it is a change, not a fixed fact)
6. It is worth reading. (worth never takes to)
5 or 6 right: good. Fewer: each one belongs to a different card, so go back to the one you missed.
activities.solo: Write the correction and then, beside it, which card the rule came from.

activities.title: Practice 7 — Find it in the account
activities.instructions:
Answer from Reading 1 only.
1. In what year did the writer qualify?
2. How many times has the work changed since then?
3. What do younger people have that the writer never had?
4. Copy a sentence in the present perfect that reaches up to now.
5. Copy a sentence in the present continuous describing a change.
6. Find the sentence with worth in it and say what form follows it.
activities.answers:
1. 1998.
2. Three times.
3. Skills the writer never had.
4. 'I have worked at the same bench for twenty years.'
   ('The work has changed three times since then' also counts.)
5. 'Younger people are arriving with skills I never had.'
   ('It is changing, which is not the same thing' also counts.)
6. 'something worth learning' — worth is followed by an -ing form.
5 or 6 right: good.
activities.solo: Read the account with a pen and mark every verb form before you answer.

quizzes.q: I have worked there for two years. What does this tell you?
options: The speaker left two years ago.
The speaker is about to start.
quizzes.why: The present perfect with for reaches up to now. I worked there for two years would mean they had left.

options: I have started this job in March.
I have never driven a van.
She has worked here since March.
quizzes.a: I have started this job in March.
quizzes.why: A definite past time forces the past simple. March has ended, however recent it feels.
yesterday is a closed time, so the past simple is the only option. The perfect cannot take a finished date.
This week is not over, so the time is still open and the perfect is right. Last week would take did.
It describes a situation in movement, which is the present continuous. rise would state it as a permanent fact.

options: I am living with my sister at the moment.
I am knowing him better now.
quizzes.a: I am knowing him better now.
quizzes.why: know is a state verb and stays simple, however temporary the state. The other three are all changes or temporary situations.
worth is one of the two adjectives that never take to. Its neighbours all do, which is why the error is so common.

quizzes.q: I am keen ___ start next month.
quizzes.why: A plain verb after keen takes to. keen ON would need the -ing form: keen on starting.

quizzes.q: He is capable of ___ the whole shift.
quizzes.why: of is a preposition, and a verb after a preposition always takes -ing.

quizzes.q: She works more carefully than he does. Which says the same thing?
options: She does not work as carefully as he does.
He does not work as carefully as she does.
He works as carefully as she does.
She works very more carefully than he does.
quizzes.a: He does not work as carefully as she does.
quizzes.why: not as ... as puts the lesser one first, so he moves to the front. The last option is wrong twice: very never precedes a comparative.

quizzes.q: He checks his work ___ carefully than she does.
quizzes.why: less is the direct opposite of more in front of an adverb. fewer counts things you can number, not manner.

options: She works most carefully than he does.
quizzes.why: much is a degree word and sits happily in front of a comparative. very never does, and better already carries the comparison.

teacherNotes.note: The present perfect FORM is taught five times below this unit: L1 U18, L2 U3 twice, L2 U8 twice and L2 U20. This unit deliberately does not re-teach the form. Cards 1 and 2 teach the three uses and the choice against the past simple, neither of which appears anywhere below.

The plan's pattern list for this unit included 'The present perfect continuous'. That form is 8Ug.07 and 9Ug.06, placed in Units 11 and 20, not here; 7Ug.06 covers present perfect simple only. The plan's list has been rewritten to match the codes placed.

Learners are usually taught that the present perfect means recent. It does not, and that rule is the direct cause of 'I have started in March'. Replace it explicitly: the question is whether the TIME is finished, not the action.

The unfinished use (job 3) has no equivalent in many first languages, so learners substitute the past simple and unintentionally tell people they have left a job they still hold. Worth checking in speech, where it costs them most.
worth + -ing fails because every adjective beside it takes to. Teach it as a two-item exception list with busy, rather than as a rule.

Several words in group 3 (accomplish, acquire, pursue) are markedly more formal than their everyday equivalents. The practice lines say so. A learner who uses them in conversation will sound stiff, which is worth naming rather than correcting later.
Speaking 2 carries 7Sc.03 alone, and it is the only pronunciation work in the unit. The weak form of have is what makes a learner's perfect sound like a perfect rather than two stressed words.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say which of the three jobs a present perfect sentence is doing.
I can choose between the present perfect and the past simple by asking whether the time has finished.
I know that a date always forces the past simple.
I can describe a situation that is changing, not just one that is fixed.
I can say whether something is temporary or permanent, using the right tense.
I can choose between to and -ing after an adjective.
I can compare how two people do something without calling either one bad at it.
I can say I have and she has so they sound natural.

assignment.title: How it has changed, and what is changing still
assignment.instructions:
Write about a job, a place or a trade you know, real or invented, in about 200 words.
Part one: what has changed. Use the present perfect at least four times, and the past simple
at least three times with a definite date each time.
Part two: what is changing now. Use the present continuous at least three times.
Part three: one sentence saying what is still worth doing, and one saying what you are keen to do next.
Use at least three of: so far, ever since, up to now, lately, already.
Then record yourself reading part two aloud, and listen for the weak have.
assignment.submissionType: Written account with a short recording
